02 · Portfolio movement and insurer behaviour¶

Questions this notebook answers (from the brief): What has changed in the portfolio, and what appears to be driving the change? Which segments or insurer behaviours deserve management attention?

Uses the in_force view from notebook 01 (duplicates removed, cancelled from inception excluded). FY26/27 contains only April to September 2026, so every year on year comparison is done half year to half year, or FY26/27 is labelled as a half.

In [1]:
import sys, warnings; sys.path.insert(0, "../src"); warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from prep import load_raw, prepare, FY_ORDER, RISK_ORDER, CT_ORDER, HALF_ORDER, market_relative_premium, in_force_at
import viz; viz.setup()
pd.set_option("display.width", 200); pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
d = prepare(load_raw("../data/raw/Business_Insight_Lead_Candidate_Assessment_Data_Set.xlsx"))
inf, clm = d["in_force"], d["claims_valid"]
priced = inf[inf.WrittenPremium_GBP > 0]       # excludes 34 zero/negative premiums from rate analysis
print(len(inf), "in force policies;", len(priced), "with a valid premium")

6099 in force policies; 6065 with a valid premium

1. Volume: the book is not growing¶

Written policies per half year have sat between 850 and 885 since the scheme's first full half. There is no growth story and no decline story. The 2026 half is in line with every previous one.

In [2]:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.bar(h.index, h.policies, color=viz.SERIES[0], width=0.7); viz.label_bars(ax)
viz.title(ax, "Policies written per half year are flat at roughly 850 to 885", "Count of in force policies by underwriting half year (H1 = Apr to Sep, H2 = Oct to Mar)")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=30); plt.savefig("../outputs/figures/portfolio_volume.png"); plt.show()
print("Policies in force at 30 Sep each year:", {y: in_force_at(inf, pd.Timestamp(y, 9, 30)) for y in [2023, 2024, 2025, 2026]})

Policies in force at 30 Sep each year: {2023: 767, 2024: 1705, 2025: 1682, 2026: 1653}

2. Rate: premium growth is price, not volume¶

Average written premium rose from £317 to £364 (about 14 percent over three years, or 4 to 5 percent a year). Because the risk and council tax mix did not move (section 3), this is rate increase, not a richer mix. Written premium total is therefore growing at roughly the same pace as rate.

3. Mix: stable on every dimension¶

If the mix were shifting towards Very High risk, higher council tax bands or Combined cover, that would explain rising premium and rising claims. It is not. Shares move by one or two points a year with no direction. This matters later: the claims increase cannot be blamed on a changing book.

4. Pricing structure: both risk band and council tax band drive premium¶

Premium rises with council tax band within each risk band, and with risk band within each council tax band. Very High risk commands roughly four times Low risk. This is a risk reflective tariff, so the scheme is already pricing by modelled risk rather than by council tax band alone. Relevant later: Very High policies pay 35 percent of premium but drive 50 percent of claims cost.

In [6]:

5. Insurers: who is doing what¶

5.1 Volume by insurer¶

Harbour (INS001) and Oak & Stone (INS002) write a third of the book between them. The small insurers are the ones moving: Rivermark (INS006) and Cedar (INS007) grew in FY24/25 then fell back; Bluegate (INS008) has shrunk every year, from 148 to 125 policies, and is on track for about 125 again in FY26/27.

5.2 Risk mix by insurer: is anyone ceding worse risk?¶

Over the whole period every insurer cedes 20 to 23 percent Very High, so no one is dumping risk at the portfolio level. By year it is noisier (these are 60 to 80 policies per cell for the small insurers). The one pattern worth a conversation: Bluegate's Very High share has climbed to 29 percent in the latest half while its volume shrinks, which is what adverse selection looks like, a smaller book skewed to the worst risk. Sample is small (63 policies), so this is a watch item, not a conclusion.

In [9]:

5.3 Pricing versus the market: Rivermark cedes cheap¶

Comparing each policy's premium to the market average for the same risk band and council tax band removes mix effects. Seven insurers sit within one percent of market, Oak & Stone 7 percent above. Rivermark (INS006) is about 12 percent below market across every band, worth about £25k of premium over the period. The gap has been closing each year (17 percent below in FY23/24, 4 percent in FY26/27), so it looks like a correction is already under way. Still worth confirming with them that the tariff is being applied correctly, because Rivermark also has the lowest claims frequency, so the cheap premium is not obviously buying good risk.

In [10]:

5.4 Cancellations¶

Cancellation after inception runs at 5 to 7 percent. Harbour (7.1 percent) and Oak & Stone and Cedar (6.4 percent) are highest; Northstar and Elmbridge lowest at under 5 percent. A two point spread on a 6 percent base is worth asking about, not acting on.

6. Takeaways for the story¶

  1. Nothing is growing except price. Flat volume, flat mix, average premium up 14 percent in three years. The scheme's written premium is rising only because rate is.
  2. The book is not getting riskier. This is important for notebook 03: whatever is happening to claims, it is not a mix effect.
  3. Two insurers to talk to. Rivermark cedes about 12 percent below the market tariff (gap closing). Bluegate is shrinking while its share of Very High risk rises. Both are small insurers, small samples, so the action is a conversation and a monitoring metric, not a sanction.
  4. Oak & Stone is 7 percent above market on price and will turn out to have the highest claims cost per policy. Worth noting as the opposite case: paying more, claiming more.

Robustness: all of section 1 to 4 is robust (large samples, issues fixed with certainty). Section 5 insurer level findings are directionally solid for the two large insurers and indicative for the small ones.
